title: Meiji Restoration
summary: In January 1868 forces from Satsuma and Choshu took the Imperial Palace in Kyoto and issued an edict restoring imperial rule, ending the Tokugawa shogunate. The Boshin War followed; Edo Castle surrendered peacefully and the last resisters yielded in June 1869. Emperor Meiji's government then abolished the feudal domains and modernised Japan.

uncertainty.note: The palace edict was in January 1868; the last bakufu supporters surrendered at Hakodate in June 1869.

as_recorded.value: In January 1868, they took control of the Imperial Palace in Kyoto and issued an edict restoring imperial rule
In 1868 the Tokugawa shogun ... lost his power and the emperor was restored

where.historical_name: Imperial Palace, Kyoto, Japan under the Tokugawa shogunate

importance.justification: Ended the Tokugawa shogunate and is widely regarded as the dividing line between traditional and modern Japan.

audience_note: Includes civil-war deaths in the Boshin War.

related.because: China's defeat in the Opium War signalled to the Japanese government that Japan was under real threat from foreign powers.

beats.caption: In January 1868 Satsuma and Choshu forces seized the Imperial Palace in Kyoto and issued an edict restoring imperial rule.
The Boshin War ended in June 1869; about 8,200 of roughly 120,000 men mobilised are thought to have died.
In 1871 the feudal domains were abolished and turned into prefectures of a unified central state.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the Boshin War casualty figure, which World History Encyclopedia introduces with "it is thought". Dating spans the January 1868 edict to the June 1869 surrender; the pin is the Kyoto palace point from Wikidata.
